facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus lived in Northwest Africa between 100 and 94 million years ago during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus (; "shark-toothed lizard") is a genus of large theropod dinosaur that lived in Northwest Africa from about 100 to 94 million years ago during the Cenomanian age of the late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The genus was first described in 1925 by Charles Depéret and Justin Savornin based on two lost fossil teeth found in Algeria.
facts.quote: The genus was first described in 1925 by French paleontologists Charles Depéret and Justin Savornin as Megalosaurus saharicus, based on two fossil teeth discovered in Algeria, which are now lost.

facts.statement: A partial skeleton was discovered in Egypt in 1914 by crews working for Ernst Stromer, who officially reported the find in 1931.
facts.quote: A partial skeleton was discovered in Egypt as early as 1914 by crews of German paleontologist Ernst Stromer, although he did not report the find until 1931.

facts.statement: The Egyptian skeleton, destroyed in World War II, was redescribed in 2025 as a distinct genus named Tameryraptor based on historical photographs.
facts.quote: Although the Egyptian skeleton was destroyed during World War II, it was redescribed as a closely related but distinct genus, Tameryraptor, based on historical photographs in 2025.

facts.statement: A large incomplete skull found in Morocco in 1995 was officially designated as the neotype for C. saharicus in 2007.
facts.quote: In 1995, a large incomplete skull attributed to C. saharicus was discovered in the Kem Kem Beds of Morocco, which was officially proposed as the neotype (specimen the species is based on) in 2007.

facts.statement: C. saharicus grew to about 12 meters in length and weighed between 5 and 7 metric tons, making it one of the largest known theropods.
facts.quote: C. saharicus reached around 12 m in length and approximately 5 - 7 MT in body mass, and was therefore one of the largest theropod dinosaurs known.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus possessed a large, lightly built skull featuring a triangular snout.
facts.quote: It had a large, lightly built skull with a triangular snout.

facts.statement: Its jaws contained sharp, recurved, and serrated teeth that closely resemble those of the great white shark, inspiring the genus name.
facts.quote: Its jaws were lined with sharp, recurved, and serrated teeth that bear striking resemblances to those of the great white shark (genus Carcharodon), the inspiration for the name.

facts.statement: The cranium was lightened by expanded depressions and holes in the bone, making it more fragile than the skulls of tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Though giant, its cranium was made lighter by greatly expanded fossae (depressions in bone) and fenestrae (holes in the skull), but this made the cranium more fragile than that of tyrannosaurids.

facts.statement: During its time, North Africa was covered in mangrove forests and wetlands, supporting high diversity of fish, crocodyliforms, and pterosaurs.
facts.quote: North Africa at the time was blanketed in mangrove forests and wetlands, creating a hotspot of fish, crocodyliforms, and pterosaur diversity.

facts.statement: Two teeth were unearthed in 1924 from wall cuts near Timimoun in French Algeria.
facts.quote: In 1924, two teeth of Carcharodontosaurus were unearthed from wall cuts in different foggaras near Timimoun, French Algeria.

facts.statement: In 1925, Depéret and Savornin described the teeth as a new theropod species named Megalosaurus saharicus.
facts.quote: In 1925, Depéret and his colleague Justin Savornin described the teeth as coming from a new species of theropod dinosaur, Megalosaurus saharicus.

facts.statement: A partial skeleton was first found near Ain Gedid, Egypt, in April 1914 by Austro-Hungarian paleontologist Richard Markgraf.
facts.quote: However, a partial skeleton later assigned to C. saharicus was first found in marls near Ain Gedid, Egypt, in early April 1914 by Austro-Hungarian paleontologist Richard Markgraf.

facts.statement: The skeleton was transported to Munich in 1922 and described by Stromer in 1931.
facts.quote: It was not until 1922 that they were transported overseas to Munich, where they were described by Stromer in 1931.

facts.statement: In 2025, the main specimen was redescribed as the holotype of a distinct genus named Tameryraptor.
facts.quote: However in 2025, this specimen was redescribed as the holotype of a distinct carcharodontosaurid genus, Tameryraptor.

facts.statement: Dozens of isolated teeth and bones from Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, and Niger were assigned to Carcharodontosaurus because it was the only known carcharodontosaurid from the region at the time.
facts.quote: Dozens of isolated teeth and bones were assigned to Carcharodontosaurus from sites across North Africa including in Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, and Niger, as it was the only carcharodontosaurid known from the region at the time.

facts.statement: Many fossils from French expeditions in North Africa were assigned to Carcharodontosaurus based on limited information, though many now belong to other genera.
facts.quote: This led many fossils of carcharodontosaurids found during French geologic expeditions to North Africa to be assigned to Carcharodontosaurus based on little information and traits now found in other genera.

facts.statement: A 2012 study suggests that isolated teeth previously assigned to Carcharodontosaurus from North Africa are now considered indeterminate due to the presence of other similar genera in the region.
facts.quote: with a 2012 study by American researcher Matthew Carrano and colleagues stated that all isolated Carcharodontosaurus teeth from the North Africa could only be considered indeterminate carcharodontosaurid teeth due to the presence of other carcharodontosaurid genera in the region.

facts.statement: In 1960, Albert-Félix de Lapparent assigned fossils from several North African formations to Carcharodontosaurus without detailed taxonomic reasoning.
facts.quote: In 1960, French paleontologist Albert-Félix de Lapparent assigned teeth and bones from outcrops of the Continental intercalaire, Echkar Formation, and Irhazer Shale in North Africa to Carcharodontosaurus, however they were assigned to the genus without detailed taxonomic discussion or reasoning.

facts.statement: In 1976, a postorbital bone and other remains were found in the Elrhaz Formation of northern Niger and assigned to the genus.
facts.quote: In 1976, a postorbital (skull bone forming right side of orbit) and several postcranial remains assigned to the genus were found in the Elrhaz Formation of northern Niger.

facts.statement: Some fossils were misidentified, such as a toe bone likely from a spinosaurid and tail vertebrae possibly from a sauropod, which were incorrectly assigned to Carcharodontosaurus.
facts.quote: Some of the fossils were misidentified, such an isolated pedal phalanx (toe bone) from the Echkar Formation was assigned to Carcharodontosaurus by Lapparent (1960), but it likely is from a spinosaurid instead, and several caudal (tail) vertebrae that may belong to a sauropod.

facts.statement: Teeth and a tail vertebra from the Chenini Formation of Tunisia were assigned to Carcharodontosaurus but are now labeled as indeterminate carcharodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Teeth and a caudal vertebra from the Chenini Formation of southern Tunisia have been assigned to Carcharodontosaurus, though these fossils are now labeled Carcharodontosauridae indet.

facts.statement: Teeth from the Gara Samani Formation were identified as Carcharodontosaurus but may actually belong to abelisaurids.
facts.quote: Additionally, from the Gara Samani Formation, previously a part of the Continental intercalaire, have been identified as Carcharodontosaurus teeth, however they may belong to abelisaurids instead.

facts.statement: The type skull was found in Cenomanian-aged rocks of the Lower Douira Formation in Errachidia, southeastern Morocco.
facts.quote: This skull was found in the Cenomanian-aged rocks of the Lower Douira Formation, Kem Kem Beds, in Errachidia, southeastern Morocco.

facts.statement: French paleontologist René Lavocat first suggested the presence of Carcharodontosaurus in the formation in 1954 based on fragmentary fossils.
facts.quote: The presence of Carcharodontosaurus in this formation was first suggested in 1954 by French palaeontologist René Lavocat on the basis on fragmentary fossils.

facts.statement: The skull, catalogued as SGM-Din 1, was initially described in 1996 by Sereno and colleagues in the journal Science.
facts.quote: The skull, since catalogued as SGM-Din 1 at the Ministry of Energy, Mines and Environment in Rabat, Morocco, was first taken to the University of Chicago, where it was initially described in 1996 by Sereno and colleagues in Science.

facts.statement: In 2007, the skull SGM-Din 1 was officially proposed as the neotype of C. saharicus because the original lectotype teeth were lost.
facts.quote: In 2007, SGM-Din 1 was officially proposed as the neotype (replacement type specimen) of C. saharicus due to the loss of the lectotype teeth and the similar age and geographic location to previously noted material.

facts.statement: The species C. iguidensis was described in 2007 by American paleontologists Steve Brusatte and Paul Sereno.
facts.quote: In 2007, another species of Carcharodontosaurus, C. iguidensis, was described by American paleontologists Steve Brusatte and Paul Sereno.

facts.statement: Fossils of C. iguidensis were uncovered in the Echkar Formation at Iguidi, Niger.
facts.quote: Fossils of C. iguidensis had been uncovered during an expedition to the rock layers of Iguidi, Niger, then identified as part of the Echkar Formation.

facts.statement: A 2016 study suggested that non-holotypic material assigned to C. iguidensis actually belongs to Sigilmassasaurus and an unrelated taxon, limiting the species to its holotype.
facts.quote: However, a 2016 paper by Italian researchers Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza and Andrea Cau identified the non-holotypic material of C. iguidensis as belonging to Sigilmassasaurus and a non-carcharodontosaurine, and therefore chose to limit C. iguidensis to the holotype pending future research.

facts.statement: A 2025 presentation suggested that C. iguidensis represents a distinct genus separate from C. saharicus based on anatomical, phylogenetic, and biogeographic differences.
facts.quote: A 2025 abstract presented by British paleontologist Charlie Scherer and colleagues at the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology annual meeting stated that C. iguidensis is from a distinct genus of carcharodontosaurid due to anatomical, phylogenetic, and biogeographic differences with C. saharicus.

facts.statement: The validity of the genus Sauroniops is debated, with some researchers considering it dubious or a synonym of C. saharicus.
facts.quote: Sauroniops validity has been questioned by several papers, with some stating that it is dubious (a species lacking diagnostic features) or a synonym of C. saharicus.

facts.statement: In 2015, a large dorsal vertebra from the Kem Kem Beds was informally named "Osteoporosia gigantea" as a potential new megaraptoran or carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: In 2015, a large neural arch (projection of bone at the top of a vertebra) of a dorsal vertebra from the Kem Kem Beds was informally described as belonging to a new genus and species of megaraptoran or carcharodontosaurid dubbed "Osteoporosia gigantea".

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the specimen informally named "Osteoporosia gigantea" may actually belong to C. saharicus or Sauroniops rather than being a distinct large genus.
facts.quote: However, it was much smaller than proposed and may belong to C. saharicus or Sauroniops based on its carcharodontosaurid traits and origin.

facts.statement: French geologist Hugues Faure collected isolated teeth resembling Carcharodontosaurus from the Akarazeras site in the Farak Formation.
facts.quote: The authors also recalled French geologist Hugues Faure's collection of isolated Carcharodontosaurus-like teeth from the Akarazeras site of the Farak Formation.

facts.statement: A maxillary tooth from the Villar del Arzobispo Formation in Spain was assigned to Carcharodontosaurus in 1966.
facts.quote: A maxillary tooth recovered from the Villar del Arzobispo Formation of Spain was assigned to Carcharodontosaurus in 1966.

facts.statement: The Spanish tooth assigned to Carcharodontosaurus lacks typical carcharodontosaurid traits and resembles other allosauroids instead.
facts.quote: However, it lacks the traits of carcharodontosaurid teeth and instead is more similar to that of other allosauroids.

facts.statement: Teeth from the Gokwe Formation in Zimbabwe were described in 1970 as similar to those of Carcharodontosaurus.
facts.quote: In a 1970 study, teeth deriving from the Gokwe Formation of Zimbabwe were described as being similar to those of Carcharodontosaurus.

facts.statement: Later studies determined that the Zimbabwean teeth previously compared to Carcharodontosaurus are indeterminate.
facts.quote: However, later studies have found these teeth to be indeterminate.

facts.statement: Teeth from Brazil's Alcantara Formation and Itapecuru Group have been placed in Carcharodontosaurus, though this is disputed due to geographic origin and lack of diagnostic features.
facts.quote: Teeth from the Alcantara Formation and the Itapecuru Group of Brazil have placed in Carcharodontosaurus, but this has been disputed based on its geographic origin and lack of diagnostic features.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Campanian Quseir Formation in western Egypt have been tentatively assigned to both Spinosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus but remain classified as indeterminate due to lack of detailed description.
facts.quote: Fossils from the Campanian Quseir Formation of western Egypt have been tentatively assigned to Spinosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus, but these specimens were never described in detail and thus classified as indeterminate.

facts.statement: Stromer originally estimated Carcharodontosaurus saharicus to be 8 to 9 meters long based on specimen SNSB-BSPG 1922 X 46, which is now known as Tameryraptor.
facts.quote: Stromer hypothesized that C. saharicus was around the same size as the tyrannosaurid Gorgosaurus, which placed it at around 8 - 9 m long, based on his specimen SNSB-BSPG 1922 X 46 (now Tameryraptor).

facts.statement: The neotype specimen of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was estimated to be 12 to 12.5 meters long and weigh between 5 and 7 metric tons.
facts.quote: The latter was estimated to be 12 - 12.5 m in length and approximately 5 - 7 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus iguidensis was smaller than C. saharicus, reaching only 10 meters in length and 4 metric tons in body mass.
facts.quote: C. iguidensis was much smaller, only reaching 10 m in length and 4 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: Since the mid-1990s, paleontologists have debated whether Tyrannosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, Giganotosaurus, or Spinosaurus was the largest theropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: Debate over what was the largest theropod dinosaur has ensued since the mid-1990s, with different researchers arguing that Tyrannosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, Giganotosaurus, or Spinosaurus was the largest theropod.

facts.statement: In 1996, Paul Sereno and colleagues estimated the skull of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus to be 1.60 meters long, similar to Giganotosaurus and possibly longer than the Tyrannosaurus specimen "Sue".
facts.quote: In 1996, Paul Sereno and colleagues estimated the skull of C. saharicus to be 1.60 m, similar in size to that of Giganotosaurus and possibly longer than that of the Tyrannosaurus specimen "Sue".

facts.statement: A 2012 study by Matthew Carrano and colleagues estimated the skull length of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus at 1.42 meters, which is slightly longer than the largest Tyrannosaurus individuals.
facts.quote: A later study by American paleontologist Matthew Carrano and colleagues in 2012 estimated the skull length of C. saharicus to be 1.42 m long, still slightly longer than that of the largest Tyrannosaurus individuals.

facts.statement: A 2007 study by François Therrien and Donald M. Henderson estimated Carcharodontosaurus at 13.3 meters long and 15.1 metric tons, surpassing both Tyrannosaurus and Giganotosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2007, Canadian researcher François Therrien and American researcher Donald M. Henderson found that Giganotosaurus would have approached 13 m in length and 13.8 MT in weight, while Carcharodontosaurus would have approached 13.3 m in length and 15.1 MT in weight (surpassing both Tyrannosaurus and Giganotosaurus).

facts.statement: The complete neotype skull of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus would measure 1.6 meters, comparable to the largest Tyrannosaurus skulls.
facts.quote: The neotype skull of C. saharicus would measure 1.6 m when complete, around the same size as the largest Tyrannosaurus skulls.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurid skulls are generally more slender and lightly built than the robust skulls of later tyrannosaurids, which evolved adaptations for crushing.
facts.quote: Skulls of carcharodontosaurids tend to be more slender and lightly built than those of later tyrannosaurids, which have robust builds and adaptations for crushing.

facts.statement: The Carcharodontosaurus skull was lighter than tyrannosaurid skulls, featuring an antorbital fenestra that made up over 30% of the total skull length and was surrounded by fossae in the maxillae, nasals, jugals, and lacrimals.
facts.quote: Its skull was lighter than that of tyrannosaurids, with the antorbital fenestra composing over 30% of the total skull length as well as being surrounded by fossae in the maxillae, nasals (nose bone), jugals (cheekbone), and lacrimals (front orbit bone).

facts.statement: The nasal bone of Carcharodontosaurus was elongated with a rugose surface likely covered by keratin sheaths, forming a horn-like structure similar to Ceratosaurus.
facts.quote: Akin to other genera, its nasal is elongated and its exposed side is covered in a rugose surface. These bumps were likely extended by keratin sheaths, creating a horn-like structure as in Ceratosaurus.

facts.statement: The lacrimal bone of Carcharodontosaurus also featured rugosity that would have been lengthened by keratin, forming a similar horn-like element.
facts.quote: A similar rugosity is found on the lacrimal which would also be lengthened by keratin, forming a similar element.

facts.statement: Sculpted exteriors on the maxillae are a unique diagnostic trait of the Carcharodontosaurus genus.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus skull has sculpted exteriors on its maxillae, which is a trait unique to the genus.

facts.statement: The lower jaw articulation in Carcharodontosaurus was positioned farther back behind the occipital condyle compared to other theropods.
facts.quote: The lower jaw articulation was placed farther back behind the occipital condyle (where the neck is attached to the skull) compared to other theropods.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus possessed a prominent nuchal crest that overhung the skull roof.
facts.quote: C. saharicus has a much more prominent nuchal crest, which overhangs the skull roof.

facts.statement: Two dentary fragments assigned to Carcharodontosaurus saharicus by Ibrahim and colleagues in 2020 feature deep and expanded tooth sockets, traits common in large theropods.
facts.quote: Two dentary (lower jaw bone) fragments which were assigned to C. saharicus by Ibrahim and colleagues in 2020 have deep and expanded alveoli (tooth sockets), traits found in other large theropods.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus teeth had numerous serrations, with 18 to 20 per centimeter in C. saharicus and up to 32 per centimeter in C. iguidensis.
facts.quote: Serrations are numerous on the anterior and posterior margins, with over 18 to 20 serrations per centimetre of edge in C. saharicus and up to 32 per centimetre in C. iguidensis.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus teeth were straight and spindle-shaped in cross-section.
facts.quote: The teeth are straight and spindle-shaped in cross-section.

facts.statement: Teeth toward the back of the Carcharodontosaurus mouth were more recurved than those at the front.
facts.quote: However, dentition towards the back of the mouth became more recurved than those towards the front of the mouth.

facts.statement: Bowed enamel wrinkles were present on both sides of the Carcharodontosaurus tooth crowns, curving toward the serrations to form a band-shape along the ends.
facts.quote: Bowed enamel wrinkles are present on both dorsoventral sides of the crowns. These wrinkles curve towards the marginal serrations, composing a band-shape along the ends.

facts.statement: The midbrain of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was angled downwards at a 45-degree angle toward the rear of the animal.
facts.quote: The midbrain is angled downwards at a 45-degree angle and towards the rear of the animal.

facts.statement: The hindbrain of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was roughly parallel to the forebrain and formed a 40-degree angle with the midbrain.
facts.quote: The hindbrain, which is roughly parallel to the forebrain and forms a roughly 40-degree angle with the midbrain.

facts.statement: Hans Larsson found that the ratio of cerebrum to total brain volume in Carcharodontosaurus was typical for a non-avian reptile.
facts.quote: Larsson found that the ratio of the cerebrum to the volume of the brain overall in Carcharodontosaurus was typical for a non-avian reptile.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus possessed a large optic nerve.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus also had a large optic nerve.

facts.statement: The three semicircular canals of the Carcharodontosaurus saharicus inner ear had a subtriangular outline when viewed from the side.
facts.quote: The three semicircular canals of the inner ear of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus—when viewed from the side—had a subtriangular outline.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus was a robust theropod with small forelimbs, an elongated tail, and a short neck.
facts.quote: Like other carcharodontosaurids, it was robust with small forelimbs, an elongated tail, and short neck.

facts.statement: Canadian researcher Dale A. Russell assigned a single cervical vertebra to the genus Carcharodontosaurus in 1996.
facts.quote: A single cervical vertebra was assigned to the genus by Canadian researcher Dale A. Russell in 1996.

facts.statement: The preserved length of the single cervical vertebra assigned to Carcharodontosaurus is 148 mm.
facts.quote: Its preserved length is 148 mm.

facts.statement: The cervical vertebra of Carcharodontosaurus lacks keels, which may be because it is an anterior cervical vertebra.
facts.quote: The centrum however lacks the keels observed in other carcharodontosaurids, possibly due to it being an anterior cervical vertebra.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus is the type genus of the family Carcharodontosauridae and the subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus is the type genus of the family Carcharodontosauridae and subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.

facts.statement: The clade Carcharodontosauridae was originally created by Stromer for Carcharodontosaurus and Bahariasaurus, but the name was not used until the late 20th century.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosauridae was a clade created by Stromer for Carcharodontosaurus and Bahariasaurus, though the name remained unused until the recognition of other members of the group in the late 20th century.

facts.statement: Between the 1950s and the 1980s, Carcharodontosaurus was classified within the family Megalosauridae.
facts.quote: From the 1950s to the 1980s, Carcharodontosaurus was classified as a member of Megalosauridae, another family of carnivorous theropods, alongside theropods like Antrodemus/Allosaurus, Megalosaurus, and Eustreptospondylus.

facts.statement: In 2004, Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues defined Carcharodontosauridae as all allosauroids more closely related to Carcharodontosaurus than to Allosaurus or Sinraptor.
facts.quote: The group was defined as all allosauroids closer to Carcharodontosaurus than Allosaurus or Sinraptor by the American paleontologist Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues in 2004.

facts.statement: Later studies suggest that Bahariasaurus is a ceratosaur, "Allosaurus" tendagurensis is an indeterminate tetanuran, and "Megalosaurus" ingens may be a species of Torvosaurus, contradicting earlier hypotheses about Carcharodontosauridae origins.
facts.quote: However, later studies have not supported these conclusions, with Bahariasaurus being suggested to be a ceratosaur, "A." tendagurensis being an indeterminate tetanuran, and "M." ingens possibly being a species of Torvosaurus.

facts.statement: A 2025 analysis by Kellermann, Cuesta, and Rauhut suggests that C. iguidensis belongs to a different genus because it is a non-carcharodontosaurine member of Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: In the phylogenetic analyses of their 2025 paper, Kellermann, Cuesta and Rauhut recovered C. iguidensis as a non-carcharodontosaurine member of the Carcharodontosauridae outside the genus Carcharodontosaurus, suggesting that this species belongs to a different genus.

facts.statement: Kellermann, Cuesta, and Rauhut named a new clade, Carcharodontosauriformes, to group carcharodontosaurids and metriacanthosaurids as sister taxa based on 2025 analyses.
facts.quote: The 2025 analyses of Kellermann, Cuesta and Rauhut found support for a sister taxon relationship of carcharodontosaurids and metriacanthosaurids, which the authors named as a new clade, Carcharodontosauriformes.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus is less well-known than other carcharodontosaurids like Meraxes and Giganotosaurus, which have nearly complete skeletons.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus is less well-known than most other carcharodontosaurids, with Meraxes and Giganotosaurus represented by nearly complete skeletons.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurians have been found from the Late Jurassic to the Mid-Cretaceous on every continent except Antarctica.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurians have been recognized from the Late Jurassic to the Mid-Cretaceous of every continent except Antarctica.

facts.statement: Research indicates that carcharodontosaurids, including Carcharodontosaurus, had a transcontinental distribution across Africa, North America, and South America by the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Sereno and colleagues found that the presence of carcharodontosaurids in Africa (Carcharodontosaurus), North America (Acrocanthosaurus), and South America (Giganotosaurus), showed the group had a transcontinental distribution by the Early Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Historical views suggested that the Cretaceous world was biogeographically separated, with Africa dominated by carcharodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Previously, it was thought that the Cretaceous world was biogeographically separated, with the northern continents being dominated by tyrannosaurids, South America by abelisaurids, and Africa by carcharodontosaurids.

facts.statement: The subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae, containing Carcharodontosaurus, was likely restricted to the southern continent of Gondwana, where it probably served as an apex predator.
facts.quote: The subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae, in which Carcharodontosaurus belongs, appears to have been restricted to the southern continent of Gondwana (formed by South America and Africa), where they were probably the apex predators.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus possessed uniquely thin and blade-like teeth that were distinct among allosauroids.
facts.quote: The dentition of allosauroids is distinct, with carcharodontosaurid teeth being uniquely thin and blade-like.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus had a high tooth replacement rate, allowing damaged teeth to be replaced easily, unlike extant bone-crushing mammals.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus also had a high tooth replacement rate, meaning that damaged teeth could be replaced easily in contrast to extant bone-crushing mammals who spend much of their energy maintaining their teeth.

facts.statement: A 2015 study analyzed the teeth of Carcharodontosaurus, Tyrannosaurus, and other dinosaurs using X-ray microscopy.
facts.quote: In a 2015 study on dinosaur tooth function, teeth of Carcharodontosaurus, Tyrannosaurus, and a variety of other dinosaurs were analyzed by X-ray microscopy.

facts.statement: A 2022 paper estimated the anterior bite force of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus at 11,312 newtons and the posterior bite force at 25,449 newtons.
facts.quote: The anterior bite force of C. saharicus was estimated in a 2022 paper to be 11,312 newtons while the posterior bite force was 25,449 newtons.

facts.statement: The lower bite force of Carcharodontosaurus compared to Tyrannosaurus implies that it likely did not eat bones.
facts.quote: This is much lower than that of Tyrannosaurus, implying that it did not eat bones.

facts.statement: Spinosaurus and Suchomimus experienced greater skull stress than Carcharodontosaurus, suggesting they could only consume light, small prey, whereas Carcharodontosaurus could bite larger items while sustaining stress.
facts.quote: However, Spinosaurus and Suchomimus experienced even greater values of stress meaning that they could only consume light, small prey instead of larger items, which the stronger skull of Carcharodontosaurus could bite while sustaining the stress.

facts.statement: Isotopic analyses suggest Carcharodontosaurus was more terrestrial than the contemporary Spinosaurus, which pursued semi-aquatic habits.
facts.quote: Isotopic analyses of the teeth of C. saharicus have found δ18O values that are higher than that of the contemporary Spinosaurus, suggesting the latter pursued semi-aquatic habits whereas Carcharodontosaurus was more terrestrial.

facts.statement: Isotopic evidence suggests Carcharodontosaurus was a homeotherm with endotherm-like thermophysiology, accumulating most of its oxygen from drinking water rather than being in water.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus was also a homeotherm with an endotherm-like thermophysiology as inferred by these isotopes meaning that most of its oxygen was accumulated by drinking water rather than being in it.

facts.statement: Daniel Chure suggested that the bony shelf above Carcharodontosaurus's orbit was used for head-butting fights.
facts.quote: In his study, Chure recounted the idea that the horns of Carnotaurus were used for "head-butting fights" and suggested that theropods with bony shelves above their orbits, like Carcharodontosaurus, did the same.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus likely functioned as an ambush predator, similar to crocodiles.
facts.quote: The range of vision seen in these allosauroids is comparable to that of crocodiles, suggesting that they were ambush predators.

facts.statement: The neotype skull of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus preserves pathologies including signs of biting, infection, and breaks.
facts.quote: The neotype skull of C. saharicus is one of many allosauroid individuals to preserve pathologies, with signs of biting, infection, and breaks observed in Allosaurus and Acrocanthosaurus among others.

facts.statement: A later study identified an unusual bony projection on the nasal of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus as a potential bite mark.
facts.quote: This skull bears a circular puncture wound in the nasal and an unusual bony projection coming from the nasal's antorbital rim, which a later study stated could be a bite mark.

facts.quote: genus_authority: Stromer, 1931

facts.quote: type_species_authority: Depéret & Savornin, 1927

facts.quote: subdivision: Carcharodontosaurus iguidensis Brusatte & Sereno, 2007

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 100 million years ago, from the Albian to early Turonian stages in what is now Africa.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus (lat. «lagarto con dientes de tiburón») es un género de dinosaurios terópodos carcarodontosáuridos, que vivieron a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 100 million years ago, entre el Albianense y Cenomaniense llegando unos pocos miles de años hasta inicios del Turoniense, en lo que hoy es África.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus shared its territory and time with Spinosaurus, another large carnivorous dinosaur.
facts.quote: Es uno de los mayores dinosaurios predadores que se conocen, y compartió el mismo territorio y la misma época con Spinosaurus, otro dinosaurio carnívoro de gran tamaño.

facts.statement: Specimens of Carcharodontosaurus discovered to date are estimated to belong to two distinct species: C. saharicus and C. iguidensis.
facts.quote: En la actualidad se estima que los especímenes descubiertos hasta la fecha pertecenen a dos especies distintas: C. saharicus y C. iguidensis.

facts.statement: Estimates for Carcharodontosaurus saharicus range from 12 to 12.5 meters in length and 6 tons in weight.
facts.quote: Las diferentes estimaciones de longitud y peso de la especie C. saharicus oscilan entre 12 a 12.5 metros de longitud y entre las 6 toneladas de peso.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus had one of the largest skulls observed in terrestrial animals, approximately 1.60 meters long.
facts.quote: Tenía uno de los mayores cráneos de los observados hasta ahora en animales terrestres, de aproximadamente 1,60 metros de largo

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus had serrated, shark-like teeth used for tearing flesh, causing prey to bleed out.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus tenía mandíbulas llenas de aserrados dientes parecidos a los de los tiburones (de ahí su nombre «lagarto con dientes de tiburón»), que tenían la función de desgarrar carne, por lo que sus presas morían desangradas

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus had front claws like butcher's hooks used to hold victims while they were torn apart by its jaws.
facts.quote: además sus patas delanteras tenían garras afiladas como garfios de carnicero para sostener a sus víctimas mientras las destrozaba con sus mandíbulas.

facts.statement: Fossilized tracks suggest Carcharodontosaurus could run at speeds of 8.5 m/s (around 30 km/h), though this estimate is now controversial.
facts.quote: Tenían como todo Carnosauria unas largas y musculosas patas traseras, y rastros fosilizados indican que podían correr hasta 8,5 m/s (alrededor de 30 km/h), aunque ahora dicha estimación es objeto de controversia.

facts.statement: Despite its size, the bite force of Carcharodontosaurus was not very high, surpassed easily by Tyrannosaurus rex and slightly by Giganotosaurus.
facts.quote: A pesar del tamaño del animal, la fuerza mandibular de Carcharodontosaurus no era muy alta, siendo superada fácilmente por Tyrannosaurus rex y ligeramente por Giganotosaurus pero similar o mayor a la de Spinosaurus.

facts.statement: A study by Donald Henderson suggests Carcharodontosaurus could physically lift animals weighing up to 424 kilograms with its jaws.
facts.quote: Un estudio realizado por Donald Henderson, conservador de dinosaurios en el Museo Tyrrell, sugiere que Carcharodontosaurus fue capaz de levantar físicamente con sus mandíbulas animales que pesaban un máximo de 424 kilogramos.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Carcharodontosaurus iguidensis measured 10 meters in length and weighed 4 tons.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul estima que C. iguidensis medía 10 metros de largo y pesaba 4 toneladas.

facts.statement: The SGM-Din 1 skull specimen of C. saharicus has a circular puncture wound in the nasal and an abnormal bony projection on the antorbital rim.
facts.quote: El espécimen SGM-Din 1, un cráneo de C. saharicus, tiene una herida punzante circular en el nasal y «una proyección anormal del hueso en el borde anteorbital».

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus fossils are known from several Cretaceous sites across North Africa.
facts.quote: Fossils of Carcharodontosaurus are known from several Cretaceous-age sites across North Africa, similar to the ranges of Spinosaurus and Deltadromeus.

facts.statement: During the Cretaceous, North Africa bordered the Tethys Sea, creating a mangrove-dominated coastal environment with vast tidal flats and waterways.
facts.quote: North Africa during this period bordered the Tethys Sea, which transformed the region into a mangrove-dominated coastal environment filled with vast tidal flats and waterways.

facts.statement: Isotopic evidence indicates that carcharodontosaurids and ceratosaurs consumed sizable terrestrial animals in the Kem Kem Beds and Elrhaz Formation.
facts.quote: Isotopic evidence supports this, which found greater quantities of sizable, terrestrial animals in the diets of carcharodontosaurids and ceratosaurs from both the Kem Kem Beds and Elrhaz Formation.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus coexisted with the sauropod Rebbachisaurus in the Kem Kem Beds.
facts.quote: It also coexisted with the sauropod Rebbachisaurus which is found in the Kem Kem Beds.

facts.statement: A tooth found alongside the holotype of Paralititan was assigned to cf. Carcharodontosaurus by Joshua Smith and colleagues in 2001.
facts.quote: A tooth found alongside the holotype of the sauropod Paralititan was assigned to cf. Carcharodontosaurus by American paleontologist Joshua Smith and colleagues in 2001.

facts.statement: Fossils in the Bahariya Formation were reassigned to Tameryraptor, though the specific tooth assigned to cf. Carcharodontosaurus has not received further attention.
facts.quote: These fossils were unearthed in a site in the Bahariya Formation, where all fossils of Carcharodontosaurus were reassigned to Tameryraptor, however this tooth specifically has not received further attention.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus was discovered by French paleontologists Charles Depéret and Justin Savornin.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus fue descubierto por los paleontólogos franceses Charles Depéret (1854-1929) y Justin Savornin (1876-1970).

facts.statement: The discovery of Carcharodontosaurus took place in North Africa in 1924.
facts.quote: El descubrimiento tuvo lugar en el norte de África en 1924

facts.statement: German paleontologist Ernst Stromer von Reichenbach described partial remains of a skull and skeleton in 1931.
facts.quote: En 1931, el paleontólogo alemán Ernst Stromer von Reichenbach describió los restos parciales de un cráneo y partes del esqueleto

facts.statement: The first Carcharodontosaurus fossil discovered was destroyed in Allied bombing raids on Germany during World War II.
facts.quote: El primer fósil de Carcharodontosaurus en haber sido descubierto fue destruido en los bombardeos que los aliados llevaron a cabo sobre Alemania durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial.

facts.statement: A more complete skull was found in the Kem Kem Formation of Morocco during an expedition led by Paul Sereno in 1995.
facts.quote: Un nuevo cráneo más completo fue encontrado en la formación Kem Kem de Marruecos durante una expedición dirigida por el paleontólogo Paul Sereno en 1995

facts.statement: The new specimen of C. saharicus is the largest found of its species and genus, with a skull measuring 1.6 meters long.
facts.quote: Este nuevo espécimen de C. saharicus es el más grande hallado de su especie y género y solo su cráneo mide 1,6 metros de largo

facts.statement: The largest known specimen is estimated to be between 12 and 12.8 meters long and weigh about 6.2 tons.
facts.quote: se estima que su tamaño fue de entre 12 y 12,8 metros de longitud y su peso en unas 6,2 toneladas

facts.statement: A second species, C. iguidensis, was reported in 2005 and formally named in 2007 based on fossils found in Niger.
facts.quote: El mismo Sereno y Stephen Brusatte en 2005 reportaron una segunda especie que fue encontrada en Níger, que difiere en algunos aspectos del maxilar y de la base del cráneo, llamada C. iguidensis en 2007.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimates that C. iguidensis was 10 meters long and weighed 4 tons.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul estima que C. iguidensis medía 10 metros de largo y pesaba 4 toneladas.

facts.statement: Fossils of Carcharodontosaurus have been found in Cenomanian rocks of the Baharija Formation in Egypt.
facts.quote: Los restos parciales de un cráneo y partes del esqueleto provenientes de rocas del Cenomaniano de la formación Baharija de Egipto

facts.statement: Remains and teeth of C. saharicus have been found in various locations across Africa, including Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia, Libya, Algeria, and Niger.
facts.quote: Restos y dientes asignados a C. saharicus han sido encontrados en gran parte de África: en la formación Baharija, en la localidad de Marsa Matruh, en Egipto, en la formación Tegana, en Ksar-es-Souk, Marruecos, en la formación Chenini, en Túnez, en Gharyan, Libia, en la formación Kem Kem de Argelia, valiatos de Adrar, Tamanrasset y Ouargla, y en Agadez, Níger.

facts.statement: Remains of C. iguidensis have only been found in the Echkar Formation in the Iguidi area of Niger.
facts.quote: los restos de C. iguidensis solo han sido encontrados hasta ahora en la formación Echkar, al oeste del oasis In Abangharit, en el área conocida como Iguidi, en Níger.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus lived from the Berriasian to the Campanian stages, between 143.1 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Berriasian to Campanian (143.1 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: The name Carcharodontosaurus comes from Greek words meaning 'sharp tooth' and 'lizard', referencing the shark genus Carcharodon.
facts.quote: El nombre Carcharodontosaurus proviene del antiguo griego καρχαρο karcharo que significa “afilado” y οδοντο odonto “diente”, que a su vez es el nombre de un género de tiburones Carcharodon, y σαυρος sauros, “lagarto”.

facts.statement: The species name was chosen because the teeth strongly resemble those of the shark genus Carcharodon.
facts.quote: Los dientes de este nuevo hallazgo coinciden con los característicos de los descritos por Depéret y Savornin, lo que llevó a Stromer a conservar el nombre de la especie pero estimando necesario erigir un nuevo género (Carcharodontosaurus saharicus) por su fuerte parecido con los dientes de los tiburones del género Carcharodon

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus is an advanced Carnosauria included in the family Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus es un Carnosauria avanzado, que se incluye dentro de la familia Carcharodontosauridae

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus is more closely related to Tyrannotitan than to Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus.
facts.quote: más cercano al Tyrannotitan, que al Giganotosaurus y Mapusaurus

facts.statement: In 2013, Novas et al. classified Carcharodontosaurus within the new subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.
facts.quote: En 2013, una revisión hecha por Novas et al., clasificó a Carcharodontosaurus dentro de una nueva subfamilia llamada Carcharodontosaurinae.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus, Tyrannotitan, Mapusaurus, and Giganotosaurus are the only genera included in the subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.
facts.quote: Por lo tanto, Carcharodontosaurus, Tyrannotitan, Mapusaurus y Giganotosaurus son los únicos géneros incluidos en esta subfamilia.

facts.statement: The midbrain of C. saharicus is inclined downward at an angle of 45 degrees toward the rear of the animal.
facts.quote: El mesencéfalo está inclinado hacia abajo en un ángulo de 45 grados y hacia la parte posterior del animal.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus had a large optic nerve.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus también tenía un nervio óptico grande.

facts.statement: The three semicircular canals of the inner ear in C. saharicus had a subtriangular outline when viewed from the side.
facts.quote: Los tres canales semicirculares del oído interno de C. saharicus, vistos desde el lado, tenían un contorno subtriangular.

facts.statement: This subtriangular inner ear configuration is present in Allosaurus, lizards, and turtles, but not in birds.
facts.quote: Esta configuración subtriangular del oído interno está presente en Allosaurus , lagartos, tortugas, pero no en aves.

facts.statement: The brain of C. saharicus would generally have been similar to that of the related dinosaur Allosaurus fragilis.
facts.quote: En general, el cerebro de C. saharicus habría sido similar al de un dinosaurio relacionado, Allosaurus fragilis.

facts.statement: Larsson found that the ratio of brain to total encephalon volume in Carcharodontosaurus was typical of a non-avian reptile.
facts.quote: Larsson encontró que la relación entre el cerebro y el volumen total del encefálo en Carcharodontosaurus era típica de un reptil no aviar.

facts.statement: The semicircular canals were very linear, which explains the pointed silhouette of the inner ear.
facts.quote: Los canales semicirculares eran en realidad muy lineales, lo que explica la silueta puntiaguda.

facts.statement: This group of large predatory dinosaurs was one of the greatest hunters of the Mesozoic, dominating southern continents from the Albian to the Cenomanian before being replaced by abelisaurids at the end of the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Este grupo de grandes dinosaurios predadores fue uno de los mayores cazadores del Mesozoico, dominaron los continentes sureños desde el Albiense (Eocarcharia) al Cenomaniense (Giganotosaurus), para ser remplazados a finales del Cretácico por los abelisáuridos.

facts.statement: Brusatte and Sereno observed that Giganotosaurus has identical teeth to C. saharicus, making the original Megalosaurus saharicus specimens indeterminate.
facts.quote: Brusatte y Sereno observaron que Giganotosaurus tiene dientes idénticos a C. saharicus, así los especímenes originales de Megalosaurus saharicus son indeterminados.
